Thank you so much for the questions. And I would now address the two questions from our distinguished delegates from the Netherlands. How do we engage on early, or how do we do early engagement together with UNICEF? And the second question on, do we refer matters to other offices when the individual may be better served at those? So for the first one, I'd like to I would just clarify that conflict happens at different levels of the organization, and the first one is it happens in people's heads. Somebody has a grievance and it's simmering and simmering and simmering, and they're not quite ready to even talk to any other person about it yet. So for those, how we need to get to them to understand early engagement is helpful is building up the trust and the confidence to actually speak to someone. Then the second level is they speak to the HR HR business partner. That's usually their main counterpart. So there we work with UNICEF, making sure that the HR business partners at all levels know that we are a free service that's available, confidentially so. Individuals do not need permission. That's, again, one thing that we keep clarifying now. The understanding differs by offices and by capacity of the HR function in those locations, so our outreach submissions to those offices help clarify that as well. We also do webinar sessions together with the HR community or with other independent offices to clarify that our motto essentially is nothing is too big or too small to come to our office for. So once people have built up the confidence and the trust that they can confidentially speak about the issue, that's where we can start with the early conflict, either preventive measures interventions, depending on what they're comfortable with. So, it is happening at different levels. We are generally partnering well with the different UNICEF offices. Again, if you go to regional events or so, when we get invited— we'd like to get invited a little bit more often, maybe— then we have an ability to clarify the rules and the services that we provide more clearly to everybody. Thank you. We try to correct this as well. That's why we introduced an after-service ombudsman survey as well to kind of probe a little bit more on what was the hesitation, was there any. And we also, of course, run into scenarios where managers prefer to address the conflicts in their teams themselves. That's also perfectly fine, but not in a rush and not unprepared. Then it tends to go the wrong way, so we try to make to make sure that everybody understands it might be better to have a conversation with our office before that happens as well in certain scenarios. But overall, it's really just clarifying that the function itself is not some faraway higher authority. I don't have any authority, in fact. It's an independent informal office. We just work in making sure people get a better sense of where their actual needs and interests lie and then find a way to addressing those rather than getting stuck on their positions and their assumptions. A lot of it is perspective changes for all levels of the organization, but for that they have to speak to someone, and that's really the early intervention. Without that, nothing really gets addressed, and it tends to simmer for so long that it then turns often into a legal dispute instead of an informally resolvable matter. On the second question, do we refer to other offices? We absolutely do. When I mention our service of discussion of options based on the issue, we will clarify every single support infrastructure piece that is available within UNICEF for that particular type of issue. If somebody mentions they're afraid of retaliation, we will absolutely clarify that they can always talk also to the ethics office and address their concern, whether it's then covered by the mandate for the ethics office to decide. We do not actively refer them without consent, so we will explain, "These are the options that you have. If you'd like me to connect to them, or if you'd like to have more information, we will give you that information." It's up to the person to then decide whether they want to take that forward, either us connecting them or they themselves reaching out to these offices. I would say the main offices that we refer people to, or where we explain how to get more information information are in the technical areas where it's about medical issues, disability, workers' compensation, social benefits, insurance issues, very technical. And one— our other close partner would be the staff well-being teams, the staff counselors. I think over 80% of our visitors have also said that they're in the conflict experience, the mental health impact detrimentally. So, of course, so we address those with the right resources. And because it's confidential, they can really speak very openly about everything that's going on. And most of us are trained coaches to make sure that we understand how to find the core of the issue rather than just the first initial explanation of what's going on. Thank you so much.
Thank you.

Closed, and the ones that are remaining are already partially addressed. Next slide. As the backdrop for UNICEF's risk profile, the report contains an overview of relevant macro trends.— and as everybody is experiencing, the world continues to be uncertain and volatile, with growing geopolitical fragmentation hindering global collaboration and multilateralism; slow economic growth with risks of a global downturn and record-high debt levels; foreign aid cuts causing organizations to merge, close, or adapt; rising inequality fueling social polarization; digital risks from misinformation, cyber threats, and AI; and increasing environmental risks. Next slide. Against that context, this year's risk report highlights the following 6 top risks. First, the risk that UNICEF may receive less funding or less flexible funding continues to be very high. The funding crisis has already hit us, but the funding environment continues to be uncertain and new risks remain. Second, this year we see global instability more broadly as a risk to our programmes and staff safety.— with more frequent and severe external shocks such as economic and financial crises, trade and supply chain disruptions, armed conflicts and violence, political polarization, and extreme weather events, which are increasingly difficult to anticipate. Then, while the FFI is an important mitigation to the funding risk, large-scale organizational change may temporarily disrupt operational capacity, programme delivery and workforce stability until those new structures, systems and ways of working become fully operational and institutionalised. The last three risks regarding misuse and aid diversion, cyber attacks and digital disruption and inadvertent harm, which includes sexual exploitation, abuse, data protection and environmental and social standards, were already there last year, but the report makes links with relevant audit findings and captures how underlying risk factors, and mitigation measures have evolved. You can find more detail for each of these risks in the reports. Next slide. Finally, as the UNICEF mandate requires the organization to operate in high-risk environments, UNICEF is in general willing to face and take the risks that are required to deliver results for children. While ensuring that robust risk management systems are in place to proactively identify, manage, and monitor those risks. We are encouraging our people to carefully balance risk versus rewards and take risks responsibly. On a high level, that means that in development contexts they require a medium risk appetite with willingness to take some risks that enable innovation and sustainability. Humanitarian contexts require a higher risk appetite in pursuit of quick and life-saving with imperfect information, but where risk management remains critical. UNICEF has a low appetite for fiduciary safeguarding and ethical risks in any context, with zero tolerance for inaction. With that, back to you, Mr. President.

Thank you.

It is our great pleasure to present the interim report of the Joint Working Group established to consider the recommendations contained in the Joint Inspection Unit review of the governance and oversight of the executive boards of UNDP, UNFPA, UNOPS, UNICEF, and UN Women of 2023. The GIU review identified 10 formal and 21 informal recommendations in 6 thematic areas: roles and responsibilities, board composition and structure, secretariat functions, meeting practices, oversight and advisory committees, and risk management. At the annual session 2024, the Executive Board's established the Joint Working Group and tasked it with reviewing all 31 recommendations and developing actionable implementation pathways. The proposals contained in the report you have before you reflect the working group's assessment of all 31 recommendations, identifying those proposed for acceptance, partial acceptance, non-acceptance, or considered completed. On the guiding principles of our work. Throughout its work, the Joint Working Group has been guided by the overarching principle of strengthening and optimizing existing mechanisms of the executive boards wherever possible before proposing the creation of new mechanisms or structures. This approach is deliberately aligned with the objectives of the UN80 Initiative, which calls for lean, efficient, and effective governance across the United Nations system. On the key findings of our preliminary report, with your permission, Mr. President, I'm happy to pass on to my co-chairs. Thank you.

Thank you very much, Annette. Good morning, colleagues. Thank you, Mr. President. On key findings and proposals, among the key proposals of the working group is the development of a comprehensive harmonized informal guidance document, a delegate's handbook, to be jointly drafted by the secretariat of all 5 organizations. The handbook would— would consolidate the roles, responsibilities, and procedures of executive board members, covering governance, oversight, risk management, and secretariat arrangements. It would address the substance of several related recommendations. It can be updated as needed, and it avoids duplication. The draft would be submitted to the executive boards for consideration, allowing for structured discussion and for for further refinement as needed. On strengthening oversight independence, a key gap identified by the JIU concerns the reporting line between internal audit and oversight committees and the executive boards. The working group proposes updating existing charters and terms of reference to establish a direct reporting line to the executive boards in addition to the executive heads, including simultaneous transmission of annual reports, post-meeting summaries, and to explicitly codify the principle of unrestricted access to oversight functions— from oversight functions to the board. The working group considers this will further strengthen the alignment and independence of audits and oversight committees. On the recommendation related to the establishment of appropriate board committees, the working group acknowledges that current arrangements are generally adequate, but recognizes the volume and technical complexity of documentation combined with limited session time may constrain the depth of the Board deliberations, particularly in oversight and finance. The Working Group proposes to explore the possible establishment of a standing advisory committee covering audit, risk, budget, and finance, composed of a limited number of members. Thank you. Member state experts with geographical representation. Further consideration, including its mandate, reporting arrangements, and interaction with the boards, will take place in the context of existing methods of work review, ensuring complementarity with existing oversight bodies and preserving the primacy of the board in decision-making. The Working Group proposes a dedicated review of the working methods of the executive boards of participating organizations, followed by periodic assessment at agreed intervals. The review would address the harmonization of work plans, the relationship between informal and formal meetings, the quality and clarity of board decisions, and the inclusiveness of member state participation. It would also provide the appropriate context for further consideration of the possible advisory subcommittee mentioned above. The Working Group proposes a formal consultation mechanism requiring executive directors to notify the boards in writing with rationale prior to the appointment, renewal, or termination of heads of independent oversight functions. Girls are especially affected by harmful practices such as child marriages, female genital mutilation, and sexual violence. More girls than boys remain out of school. Among children with disabilities, girls face an even higher risk of exclusion. At the same time, we are encouraged by the progress UNICEF reports in several areas. For example, service— services to prevent and respond to FGM have expanded significantly. More countries are introducing family-friendly care policies. Partnerships with women's and girls' rights organizations have strengthened. These results show that progress is possible when gender equality is prioritized and when governments and communities engage. We strongly support UNICEF's focus on adolescent girls as an accelerator for change in the strategic plan. Investing in adolescent girls' sexual and reproductive health and rights, the right to not be forced into child or early marriage, and their access to comprehensive sexuality education— education and training has wide positive effects in societies. The transformative approach that UNICEF employs by engaging with men and boys on gender equality is important. Investing in innovation is also key. We welcome UNICEF's venture fund FemTech initiative. We would welcome further clarification on the following points. In the context of shrinking resources, how is UNICEF managing funding constraints and mitigating the impact on its gender equality efforts? And while we welcome the increase in expenditures making a principal contribution to gender equality to 12% in 2025. How does UNICEF plan to reach the target of at least 15% principal gender expenditure in the next planning cycle? And how and by when will UNICEF ensure that all country offices meet gender action plan standards? What consequences exist for non-compliance offices and are gap standards linked to performance management? In closing, we would like to stress the importance of UNICEF continuing to prioritize and mainstream gender equality across its work at a time of significant pushback. The leadership of UNICEF representatives at all levels must speak out, champion gender equality and SRHR, and holding partners accountable. It is critical. Thank you.

The annual report shows strong progress. Over half of country offices are integrating gender equality into preparedness and conducting rapid gender analyses to inform program delivery. Almost 11 million girls, boys, and women have been reached with gender-based violence services, exceeding targets. Partnerships have also been established with diverse local and grassroots actors, including girls' and women's rights groups. Looking ahead, we would like to see a stronger focus on girls and women with disabilities who face heightened risks of exclusion, discrimination, and violence in crises. Better use of disaggregated data will be essential. Thank you. We are pleased to note the modest improvements in funding for women-led organizations, and we encourage further increases in line with the principles of locally-led action and equitable partnerships. We also call for greater attention to the safety and protection of female frontline workers, including those in humanitarian and health roles, who face disproportionate risks. I thank the distinguished representative of the United Kingdom. Next speaker is Mexico.

Thank you very much, Mr. President and Director Rumble. Mexico welcomes the annual report on the implementation of the UNICEF Gender Action Plan for 2022 to 2025. These efforts will lead to greater results-level progress and will contribute to consolidating lasting achievements for girls and women. Mr. President, for Mexico, gender equality is an essential precondition for peace and sustainable development. For this reason, we welcome the fact that the plan of action recognizes the importance of designing measures that address the differentiated impacts that are faced by children and adolescents In this context, Mexico believes it's essential to continue moving ahead to eliminate all forms of violence against girls and adolescents. The fact that globally 1 out of every 5 girls and women have been the victim of sexual violence in childhood bears out the need to strengthen protection systems. For Mexico, it's also essential to address the disproportionate burden of care work falling on women and girls because the care agenda is essential in my country. Finally, Mexico agrees with the concern at the shrinking resources for gender equality and the empowerment of adolescents. Because we believe that investing in equality is not only vital in human rights, but also essential to ensuring that no one is left behind. Thank you.

Mr. President, the United States supports positive outcomes for boys and girls. We welcome UNICEF's work to delay child marriage, adulthood, end female genital mutilation, increase girls' education access, strengthen maternal and newborn health, streamline immunization for children, and combat sexual violence against boys and girls. While our outputs are strong, uneven progress persists. We encourage UNICEF to identify evidence-based, measurable approaches that deliver results for girls and women most in need. The United States believes that strong families are the foundation of children's well-being and that fathers and positive male role models are essential to that foundation, not an obstacle to it. We welcome the report's recognition of men and boys engaged as caregivers and partners. Men and boys are allies in advancing the welfare of women and girls, and the welfare of boys themselves deserve the same attention. At the same time, the United States must clearly note elements of the report that do not align with U.S. policy. The document makes repeated use of terminology and concepts that the United States does not— Recognize. Recognize and cannot accept, including expansive and ambiguous gender frameworks, gender-responsive systems, sexual and reproductive health, and references to the SDGs or 2030 Agenda. These terms are inconsistent with U.S. policy, which requires clear, biologically grounded language and strict focus on equality between women and men and on the safety and well-being of boys and girls. We also deeply concerned about the programmatic expansions described in the reports, such as broad social norms and transformations, systems-wide behavioral engineering and institutional benchmarks that condition performance on adherence to these problematic ideological frameworks. The United States remains committed to working constructively with UNICEF and the Board to advance effective, measurable health for children, anchored in the welfare of children and the strength of families. Thank you.

I can give an example of Kenya, where a cost-benefit analysis conducted by a university, by UNICEF, by the government of Kenya helped to then really supercharge financing from both the Kenyan government as well as international donors to address adolescent girls' rights and health across parenting, education, and skills programs. Merci, Monsieur le Président. Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, distinguished delegates, Madam Executive Director, distinguished colleagues, ladies and gentlemen. Since my intervention last year, UNICEF has been undergoing a profound transformation. What was initially perceived as concerns linked to change has for many colleagues transformed into a prolonged a sense of uncertainty and fatigue as the FutureFocus Initiative, office consolidations, and workforce adjustments continue to reshape the way we work. It should be noted that the GSA has benefited from generally constructive exchanges with management.

Thank you.

Providing an important space for dialogue at a key moment of organizational transformation. Across various duty stations, colleagues are facing increased workloads, reduced staffing, shorter-term contracts, and evolving structures In a context marked by uncertainty linked to successive budget cycles, this transformation has a real human impact with growing signs of stress and strain on both physical and mental health. Many colleagues feel pushed beyond sustainable limits while continuing to strive to maintain the quality and commitment required by UNICEF's mission, we are observing an alarming decline in colleagues' willingness to take on staff representative roles, linked both to fears of potential personal or professional consequences and to the increasing burden of workload and pressure. This trend is particularly worrying as staff representation, a historic pillar of a healthy organizational culture and of the organization's strength, is gradually being eroded. This represents a major risk at a time when it is more than necessary than ever before We must continue to strengthen transparency through sustained and coherent communication and through consistent engagement through country office management teams. Colleagues need predictable, timely, and honest information, not only about decisions that are taken, but also about the justifications underpinning those decisions. We must not lose sight of the importance of safety. Last year, we lost colleagues amid context of insecurity. These losses serve as a reminder of the fact that the work of UNICEF is not only demanding, but also dangerous. The role of— Security management must remain central. Colleagues must be able to rely on the organization's unwavering commitment to their safety. Beyond operational systems, there is a deeper need for leadership and for a robust accountability framework ensuring that Values, responsibilities, and behaviors are consistently upheld across the organization. While staff support services remain essential, they alone are not sufficient. Every leader has a responsibility to create environments where staff and staff representatives feel respected, heard, and supported. Compassionate leadership is not an option. Compassionate leadership is a prerequisite for resilience. We must pay attention, particular attention, to early and mid-career staff. Who joined UNICEF with a strong sense of mission, but people who are now facing extremely limited prospects. They're facing uncertainty and in certain cases, reduced confidence in their future within the organization. Without proactive investment in their development and retention, We are liable to weaken the very foundation of UNICEF's workforce. I wish to thank you for your partnership and for your ongoing support for UNICEF personnel. Mr. Chairman, I yield the floor.

Thank you. Mr. President, Madam Executive Director, distinguished staff association representatives, distinguished colleagues. I deliver this statement on behalf of the following cross-regional list of member states: Belgium, Bulgaria, Canada, Denmark, Equatorial Guinea, Eritrea, Estonia, Eswatini, Finland, Germany, Ireland, Japan, Lesotho, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, Mauritania, the Kingdom of the Netherlands, Nigeria, Norway, Senegal, Sweden, United Republic of Tanzania, Ukraine, and my own country, Iceland. We thank the chair of the the Global Staff Association for a frank and thoughtful intervention. We commend the courage of staff representatives who speak up at a time of profound change for UNICEF. UNICEF's greatest asset is its people. The concern voiced today— concerns voiced today go to the core of UNICEF's ability to deliver for children. As strong supporters of of UNICEF, we take these signals very seriously. We recognize that the Future Focus Initiative, office consolidations, and workforce adjustments are taking place in a context of tight and often unpredictable funding. We also recognize the need for UNICEF to adapt in order to remain effective and efficient. But reform cannot come at the expense of the well-being and trust of staff. If staff are let go due to these realities, it is key that it is done in a dignified and compassionate manner. For us, a fit-to-purpose UNICEF is one that is also fit for its staff. Allow me to highlight 4 points. First, on transparency and communication. We fully support the call for predictable, timely, and honest communication. with staff, including at country level. Uncertainty is sometimes unavoidable. Opacity is not. We encourage UNICEF management to systematically explain the rationale for decisions, to engage staff early in change processes, and to ensure that feedback loops are in place. Direct staff consultation is key. Feedback mechanisms should be safe accessible and followed by visible action. Where staff have experienced challenges or harm as a result of reforms, there should be avenues for redress and course correction. The Board stands ready to support management in strengthening this culture of open dialogue. Second, on staff representation. We attach great importance to strong, independent staff representation as a cornerstone of a healthy organizational culture. We are concerned by the reported decline in willingness to take on staff representative roles and by fears of potential repercussions. We expect UNICEF to uphold the freedom and protection of staff representatives and to ensure that they can perform their roles without fear and with adequate time and recognition. We would welcome for further reporting to the Board on how these safeguards are being implemented in practice. Third, on safety and duty of care, we express deep appreciation for the dedication and professionalism of UNICEF staff. We are acutely aware that many colleagues face repeated emergency deployments, long separations from family, and exposure to trauma and moral distress. National UNICEF staff in particular often remain in duty stations throughout crisis, bearing the brunt of insecurity and economic hardship. Many UNICEF staff work in insecure contexts and face risks on a daily basis. We pay tribute to the UNICEF colleagues who lost their lives. We expect that security management and duty of care remain central in UNICEF's operations and that lessons learned from security incidents are translated into concrete improvements. Fourth, on leadership, accountability, and career perspectives. We strongly endorse the staff association's call for compassionate leadership and a robust accountability framework. Managers at all levels must model the values of the organization and create an environment where staff feel respected, heard,— and supported. We are particularly attentive to the situation of early and mid-career staff, whose motivation and development are essential to UNICEF's future. We encourage UNICEF to invest in clear career paths, learning opportunities, and transparent talent management, and to share with the Board how these issues are being addressed within the broader reform. Mr. President, we will continue to be a We are a committed partner to UNICEF and its staff. We support the necessary transformation of the organization, but we expect this to be a transformation with staff, not a transformation imposed on staff. We expect continued structured dialogue between management and the staff association at global, regional, and country levels. We look forward to hearing at future sessions of this board how the concerns raised today have been translated into concrete action. Thank you.
